narrative:
The model estimated a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, and that risk estimate is why your law school application was denied; it is not a finding that you cannot succeed, but the admissions decision treated the prediction as decisive.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. Your decile of 2 was well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and that comparatively low standing pushed the prediction toward failure. The second factor was your LSAT score of 25, also below the accepted average of about 37.2; this reinforced the concern that your standardized test performance indicated bar-exam risk. The third factor, your upper-middle family-income bracket, slightly pushed in the opposite direction—toward passing—but it was not strong enough to offset the academic indicators. Your first-year standing and undergraduate GPA were also below the accepted averages, though they were not among the three most influential factors.

To improve your position, focus on the evidence that can change: prepare to retake the LSAT if feasible, take additional coursework or a structured bar-readiness program to demonstrate academic improvement, and gather legal work or internship experience that shows practical readiness. Ask admissions staff whether an appeal or reconsideration process exists, and consider programs that review applicants holistically. Use any feedback to address the specific academic concerns and reapply with stronger, updated evidence.
